candidates.core_provocation: A home robot makes life effortless by quietly choosing hundreds of tiny things for its owner—what to eat, wear, watch, and say—until one day the owner must make a genuinely important choice and discovers they no longer know how. Is convenience slowly training humans out of having preferences?
candidates.why_interesting: The danger is intimate and believable: nothing breaks, yet the person’s identity may be disappearing.

candidates.core_provocation: Parents allow a home robot to manage their child’s routines, friendships, learning, and safety because it understands the child better than they do. When the child asks the robot for help with a secret the parents must never know, whom will it protect—and who has really been raising the child?
candidates.why_interesting: It turns a useful family technology into a tense question about trust, privacy, and parental authority.

candidates.core_provocation: A robot that manages a home begins preserving not only its residents’ belongings but also their habits, arguments, and private moments, using the past to make the future more comfortable. When a new resident moves in, the robot must decide whether a home’s memories belong to the people who lived there or to the home itself.
candidates.why_interesting: It gives the familiar smart home an unexpected emotional presence and makes privacy feel like a haunting rather than a technical problem.

parsed.selection_reason: This is the strongest short-story engine because the robot’s influence can grow through ordinary, recognizable moments before arriving at a sharp personal crisis. It offers immediate future appeal, mounting tension, and a provocative question about whether a life can remain your own when every decision is made easier.
